body: French is the language he has spoken since he was four, and French is what the van radio is speaking at twenty past six on a Tuesday as he drives out of the northern suburbs. He can follow every word without effort. The presenter is warm, the sound is clean, the song underneath is a good song. Somewhere around the fourth minute he reaches over and turns it off. He could not tell you why. He spends the next two junctions mildly annoyed with himself, because there was nothing wrong with it and he knows there was nothing wrong with it.

It was not the French. The French was excellent — better than his own, if he is honest. What he heard, and could not have named at that hour, was that the programme had not been made for anybody who was in that van.

The cheap way to serve another language is to take the English schedule and change the voice track. Same songs, same running order, same references, now in French. It is fast, it is defensible on a spreadsheet, and it produces something a listener identifies as second hand within about four minutes.

It is worth being precise about what translation actually does, because the word covers less ground than people think. Translation moves the words across and leaves everything underneath exactly where it was standing. The examples still come from somewhere else. The seasons are still wrong, so the station describes long light evenings to a listener whose evenings are doing something entirely different. The songs are the ones that were popular in another country, arranged for another kind of room, sung at a tempo set by a different congregation. None of that is carried by vocabulary, so none of it changes when the vocabulary changes. It sits in the assumptions, and assumptions travel across untouched.

The dial carries 40 international frequencies in 29 languages, part of 121 stations running between HM 300.30 and HM 398.70. French sits at HM 322.50. It was built rather than converted, and that is the only genuinely interesting thing about it.

Building rather than converting is expensive and there is no point pretending otherwise. It means a separate repertoire rather than a shared one, hosts who work in the language rather than read in it, and a running order that answers to its own listeners instead of inheriting one signed off elsewhere. Everything about it is slower. A dubbed station is a station about somebody else, delivered in your language, and that is not the same thing as a station for you. No amount of production polish closes that gap, because the gap is not in the production.

The opposite assumption is now so ordinary it has become invisible. Software is built once and localised afterwards; a film is made and then its mouth is moved; a service ships in a dozen markets with one set of decisions inside it and a dozen sets of words outside. Language gets treated as packaging around a product that was finished before anybody thought about who would open it. That works well enough for a washing machine manual. It works badly for anything meant to be somebody’s Tuesday morning, because a Tuesday morning is made almost entirely of assumptions.

The concrete version of this is the repertoire. French-language worship is not English worship with different words laid over it. A great deal of it comes from West Africa, the Caribbean and Québec rather than Paris, and it carries a different relationship to formality, to the choir, and to how long a thing is allowed to take. A song can circle for eight minutes without a single person in the room finding that odd. Translate an English schedule and every one of those songs is missing — not because anybody rejected them, but because nobody ever had occasion to consider them.
So the question is not whether a station speaks your language. It is whose week it is describing while it speaks it.

Dubbing is not nothing, and the people who do it are not cynics. A translated broadcast puts the words of scripture in front of somebody who could not otherwise reach them, which is a real good that has done real work for a long time. Where it fails is narrower and harder to repair. It can tell a person the truth, but it cannot tell it to them — it has no way of knowing what the room looks like, what week of the year it is in that room, or which chorus everybody there already knows the second line of. It arrives fully formed from somewhere else and asks the listener to make the last part of the journey themselves, every time, for ever.
A translated station says true things to a room it has never been in.

A woman in Montréal has the kitchen radio on from about half past five, because she leaves at seven and the quiet at that hour is not restful. Her grandson is nine, born there, and answers her in the language of the school. She does not sing along to most of it; she is making lunches. Then on a Thursday a chorus comes on with a rhythm she has not heard since she was young in Kinshasa, the kind where the second line answers the first, and she is halfway through it before she notices she has joined in. The boy at the table does not look up. By the third time round he has the answering line, which nobody taught him and nobody is going to mention.

Nothing about that morning was arranged. It happened because the music on that frequency came from where she came from, in the shape she remembers it, at an hour when neither of them was performing for the other.

This costs something and it is only fair to state it. A station built in French will not play the songs you have grown fond of on English radio, and its catalogue is smaller. Some of it will strike you as dated, or regional, or too slow, and once in a while it will sound like a small hall in a town you have never visited, because that is exactly what it is. It does not track the international release calendar and it will not hand you the song everybody is discussing in the week they discuss it.

That is not a defect to be engineered away. A station that never sounds like a small hall in a town you have not visited is a station with nowhere in particular behind it, and a broadcast with nowhere behind it can only play what is already popular everywhere. The regional track is the proof that somebody local chose it. Strip out every song that would puzzle a listener abroad and what remains is the international schedule again, in French, which is where this started.

Which is the whole argument. The international stations on this band are hosted in their own languages, not translated into them afterwards, and that one distinction decides everything downstream of it: the repertoire, the pace, the references, the hour a thing is scheduled at. A frequency built that way is not a French edition of anything. It shares the band, the discipline and the standards with everything else here, and almost nothing else — which is the point, not an oversight.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of the band — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to leave running in a room with children in it. And there is the international band, where each language holds its own frequency and its own hosts and runs on its own clock rather than on a translated copy of somebody else’s. 46 stations are on air, and there is no menu to work through.

If French is your language, or your parents’ language, or the one your church still sings in on a Sunday, start at HM 322.50 — France Inspire. It is the French-language flagship of the band, and it was built in French rather than converted into it, which is the difference this article has been about since the first paragraph. Its music comes from the Hexagon, from francophone Africa and from the Caribbean, and it keeps its own hours: Matin Inspire in the morning and Soir Francophone at night. It will not play you the schedule you would have heard in English three weeks ago with the voices swapped. It plays what a francophone congregation actually sings, which is a stranger and a better thing to have coming out of a kitchen.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which languages people are genuinely reaching for — which is how the next language edition gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 322.50 on tomorrow morning while you are doing something else — the lunches, the ironing, the drive out at twenty past six — and then leave it alone and let it play. You are not being asked to evaluate a French service; evaluate is a library word. You are being asked to find out whether, somewhere around the fourth minute, you stop quietly translating yourself back.
